facts.fact_text: On 22 February 1999 the applicant and two other persons, allegedly acting on behalf of the Komunenergiya staff, gave a written notice to the Mayor of Rivne.
The written notice of 22 February 1999 to the Mayor of Rivne stated that employees of Komunenergiya would picket the management of Komunenergiya at 7.30 a.m. on 3 March 1999.
The written notice of 22 February 1999 to the Mayor of Rivne stated that the reason for the picket was non-payment of salary from August 1998 to February 1999.
On 3 March 1999 the applicant and some seventy other persons took part in a picket in front of Komunenergiya's main office.
At the picket on 3 March 1999, participants expressed concerns that the management of Komunenergiya did not ensure timely payment of salaries.
At the picket on 3 March 1999, participants expressed concerns that the director of Komunenergiya had misappropriated company funds.
On 10 March 1999 the applicant was dismissed from work for systematic breach of her duties of employment pursuant to Article 40 § 3 of the Labour Code of 1971.
On 29 March 1999 the applicant instituted proceedings in the Rivne Court seeking reinstatement in her position at Komunenergiya.
On 29 March 1999 the applicant instituted proceedings in the Rivne Court seeking recovery of salary arrears.
In its judgment of 21 June 2000, the Rivne Court concluded that the applicant had been lawfully dismissed pursuant to Article 40 § 3 of the Labour Code of 1971.
In its judgment of 21 June 2000, the Rivne Court held that the applicant's submissions concerning a labour dispute between the management and staff were unsubstantiated.
On 11 September 2000 the Rivne Regional Court quashed the judgment of the Rivne Court of 21 June 2000 and remitted the case for fresh consideration.
On 10 July 2001 the Rivne Court dismissed the applicant's claim on the same grounds as those given in its judgment of 21 June 2000.
By a decision of 3 January 2002, the Rivne Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's appeal as unsubstantiated and upheld the findings of the Rivne Court.
By a decision of 13 August 2002, the Supreme Court of Ukraine dismissed the applicant's appeal as unsubstantiated and upheld the findings of the Rivne Court.
Article 44 of the Constitution of Ukraine provides that employees have the right to strike in order to protect their economic and social interests.

Article 44 of the Constitution of Ukraine provides that the procedure for exercising the right to strike shall be established by law, taking into account the need to ensure national security, the protection of health, and the rights and freedoms of other persons.
Article 44 of the Constitution of Ukraine provides that no one shall be forced to participate or to not participate in a strike.
Article 44 of the Constitution of Ukraine provides that a strike may only be prohibited on the basis of law.

Article 40 § 3 of the Labour Code of 1971 provides that a labour contract of indefinite duration may be discontinued by an employer in cases of systematic and unjustified failure by an employee to fulfil his duties under the labour contract or staff regulations, if there were earlier disciplinary or public sanctions imposed on him.

Article 151 of the Labour Code of 1971 provides that if no new disciplinary sanction is imposed on an employee within a year of the imposition of a previous disciplinary sanction, he is considered to have not been subjected to a disciplinary sanction.

Section 3 of the Resolution of Labour Disputes (Procedure) Act of 3 March 1998 provides that parties to a collective labour dispute at an occupational level include employees or a trade union or another organisation authorised by employees to represent their interests, and the owner of an enterprise or the employer's representative.

Section 3 of the Resolution of Labour Disputes (Procedure) Act of 3 March 1998 provides that a body authorised by employees to represent their interests shall be the only authorised representative of employees during the time such a dispute exists.

Section 17 of the Resolution of Labour Disputes (Procedure) Act of 3 March 1998 defines a strike as a temporary, collective and voluntary cessation of work by employees with the aim of resolution of a collective labour dispute.

Section 17 of the Resolution of Labour Disputes (Procedure) Act of 3 March 1998 provides that striking shall be an extreme means of resolution of a collective labour dispute when all other possibilities of such resolution have been exhausted and the employer refuses to allow the claims of employees or of a body authorised by them, or of a trade union, or of an association of trade unions or of a body authorised by them.

Section 18 of the Resolution of Labour Disputes (Procedure) Act of 3 March 1998 provides that pursuant to Article 44 of the Constitution of Ukraine employees have the right to strike in order to protect their economic and social interests.

Section 18 of the Resolution of Labour Disputes (Procedure) Act of 3 March 1998 provides that a strike may be commenced if conciliatory procedures have not led to the settlement of a collective labour dispute, or if the employer avoids conciliatory procedures, or does not comply with an agreement reached in the course of the resolution of a collective labour dispute.

Section 19 of the Resolution of Labour Disputes (Procedure) Act of 3 March 1998 provides that a decision to announce a strike at an enterprise shall be taken by the majority of employees at a general assembly or conference of employees, or by two-thirds of delegates to the conference, upon a request of a trade union or another association of employees authorised to represent the interests of employees, and that minutes must be drawn up reflecting such a decision.
Section 19 of the Resolution of Labour Disputes (Procedure) Act of 3 March 1998 provides that no one shall be forced to participate or to not participate in a strike.

Section 19 of the Resolution of Labour Disputes (Procedure) Act of 3 March 1998 provides that a body or person leading a strike shall inform the employer no later than seven days before the commencement of a strike, or no later than fifteen days if the decision to strike concerns a non-stop work process.

Section 19 of the Resolution of Labour Disputes (Procedure) Act of 3 March 1998 provides that the owner or his representative shall inform, as soon as possible, suppliers, consumers, transport organisations, and other interested enterprises about the employees' decision to announce a strike.

Section 19 of the Resolution of Labour Disputes (Procedure) Act of 3 March 1998 provides that a body or person leading a strike shall determine the place of the strike in agreement with the owner or his representative.

Section 19 of the Resolution of Labour Disputes (Procedure) Act of 3 March 1998 provides that if an assembly, meeting, or a picket takes place outside the enterprise, the body or person leading the strike shall inform the local authority no later than three days before it takes place.

Section 23 of the Resolution of Labour Disputes (Procedure) Act of 3 March 1998 provides that an application by the employer seeking to have a strike declared unlawful shall be considered by a court within seven days.

Section 23 of the Resolution of Labour Disputes (Procedure) Act of 3 March 1998 provides that a court's judgment declaring a strike unlawful obliges persons taking part in the strike to adopt a decision discontinuing or cancelling the announced strike, and obliges employees to return to work no later than the next day after the body or person leading the strike is served with a copy of the court's judgment.

Section 27 of the Resolution of Labour Disputes (Procedure) Act of 3 March 1998 provides that employees' participation in a strike, with the exception of strikes declared unlawful by a court, shall not be considered as a violation of work discipline and may not serve as a ground for disciplinary action.

Section 28 of the Resolution of Labour Disputes (Procedure) Act of 3 March 1998 provides that organisation of, or participation in, a strike declared unlawful by a court shall constitute a violation of work discipline.
Section 28 of the Resolution of Labour Disputes (Procedure) Act of 3 March 1998 provides that employees shall not be remunerated for the time during which they take part in a strike.

Section 28 of the Resolution of Labour Disputes (Procedure) Act of 3 March 1998 provides that the time during which an employee takes part in a strike declared unlawful by a court shall not be included in the period of his general and uninterrupted length of service.

Resolution No. 9 of the Plenary Supreme Court of Ukraine of 6 November 1992 concerning courts' practice of consideration of labour disputes provides that an employee may be dismissed pursuant to Article 40 § 3 of the Labour Code of 1971 for an offence committed at work only after disciplinary or public sanctions for unjustified breach of his duties under the labour contract or staff regulations have been imposed on him.

Resolution No. 9 of the Plenary Supreme Court of Ukraine of 6 November 1992 provides that in cases of dismissal under Article 40 § 3 of the Labour Code of 1971, only the disciplinary sanctions which are envisaged by law and are still in force pursuant to Article 151 of the Labour Code of 1971 shall be taken into account.
According to the applicant, she and many of her colleagues had not received the salary due to them for the period of August–December 1998 during which they had worked at Rivneteplokomunenergo.
In February 1999 a number of Komunenergiya employees met to discuss possible solutions to the problem of unpaid salary for the period August–December 1998.
The Komunenergiya employees who met in February 1999 agreed to form a trade union at Komunenergiya.
The Komunenergiya employees who met in February 1999 agreed to organise a picket.
